THE PROBLEM
Fluent on paper.
Hesitant
in the room.
Your people passed the test. They read the contracts, they follow the calls. But in the negotiation, the board update, the difficult client conversation, they hesitate. They soften when they should hold firm, or push when they should hedge. The deal doesn't fail on grammar. It fails on tone.
That gap isn't vocabulary. It's pragmatics, register, and timing: the layer standard courses rarely teach, because it's harder to test and harder to sell. It's also the layer your senior people are judged on, in every room that matters.
Built for the moment the meeting gets real, not the moment the test ends.
THE FOUNDER
Founded by a teacher.
One method
, 25 years in.
Concept was founded by Pedro Gigollotti, who has taught professional communication for 25 years in six countries: Brazil, the USA, England, Ireland, Malta, and Italy. That experience is why Concept can teach how English changes between a London boardroom, a New York sales call, and a Milan negotiation.
Pedro designed the Concept method and directs every program. He also works in teacher training, Cambridge examination preparation, and syllabus design. Every Concept lesson follows the method he designed, the same way each time.
Teacher training
Pedro trains teachers in the method, so it is taught precisely and never improvised.
Cambridge examinations
Deep experience preparing candidates for Cambridge and ALTE-benchmarked assessment.

THE METHOD
A method with a mechanism, not just a name.
Lexical Approach
Language is taught the way it's actually used, as chunks and collocations rather than isolated grammar. Roots, trunk, branches, leaves: every lesson grows from real context, not a word list.
Constructivism
Students reason through grammar by comparing it to their own native language, and reach conclusions themselves. A rule you derive sticks longer than one you're handed.
Psycholinguistics
Knowing the language is useless if your brain cannot retrieve it under pressure. We analyze cognitive load, working memory limits, and mother-tongue interference to build rapid automaticity. We don't just train what you say; we train how your brain accesses it when the stakes are high.
THE TRIPLE A CYCLE. EVERY LESSON.
Where the difference
actually
shows up.
A1
Access
Students meet new language in a real, unmodified context: an email, a call, a negotiation.
A2
Analysis
The key step. Every expression is mapped onto five registers, from frozen to intimate, so students learn exactly when a phrase costs them credibility.
A3
Activation
That language gets used right away, in a scenario close to what the student will actually face at work.
Most methods stop at meaning. Ours doesn't stop until the register is right.
LEVELS
Levels the market already recognizes.
Every program is mapped directly onto the CEFR scale (A1 to C2) and tested against Cambridge and ALTE benchmarks. Progress is measured against a global standard, not an internal scorecard.

THE LEARNING
Pace tied to progress, not the calendar.
Hours are structured around ALTE-defined benchmarks. A student who reaches a stage's goals faster than scheduled advances immediately, with no waiting on a fixed calendar built for someone else's pace.
Level reached over 6 months
Illustrative: how progress-based pacing compares with a fixed calendar.
Fixed-calendar course
Concept (progress-based)
Points per skill, per assessment
Concept's actual assessment weighting, applied after every lesson.
We weight speaking and listening higher on purpose. Speaking and understanding in real time is what separates fluency from a passed test. Every student is assessed after every lesson, and you get a monthly report with hours, attendance, the trend for each skill, and written notes.

QUESTIONS
What people ask before they start
What is Concept?
Concept, also called The Concept Method, is a business English training company. It trains professionals who already speak English to use it with confidence at work.
Who is it for?
Individuals and teams: leadership and client-facing teams, international and expanding companies, and HR and L&D departments that need progress they can report.
How does the method work?
Every lesson follows three steps: Access, Analysis, and Activation. The method teaches what standard courses skip: register, pragmatics, and timing under pressure.
Where does Concept teach?
Concept works with professionals in São Paulo, Rome, and Milan. Programs run online, in person, or blended, for individuals or full departments.
How is progress measured?
Every program is mapped to the CEFR scale, from A1 to C2, and tested against Cambridge and ALTE benchmarks. Every student is assessed after every lesson, and you get a monthly report.
What happens between lessons?
Learners practice in the Concept Coach app with the Concept team: six AI coaches built on the Concept method and led by Netto, director of studies.
Are there books?
Yes. Professional English Practice is a series of five books, from A1 to C2, with one book on phrasal verbs. Calibrated Speech is a pronunciation manual for Brazilian speakers of American English.
How do I start?
With a free 45-minute diagnostic call. We speak with one or two of your people, and you get a written diagnosis with the current CEFR level and the specific gaps. Then you decide.

Netto
DIRECTOR OF STUDIES
REGISTER
Victor Hugo
“Read the room, then hit send.”
Victor Hugo shows your people what a sentence tells the person reading it, from a client email to a quick Slack thread. They choose the version. He makes sure they know why.
Hear Victor Hugo
CHECK
Who is reading?
Client
Manager
Leadership
Slack
We need the contract signed by Friday.
WHAT THIS TELLS A CLIENT
Correct, and it reads as an order. The client hears your deadline before their reason to sign.
Would it be possible to have the contract signed by Friday?
Reads as a request. The client has room to say yes.
Could we aim to have it signed by Friday?
Makes the deadline shared work.
You know this client. Your call.
GRAMMAR AND PUNCTUATION
Luana
“Every comma counts.”
Luana works on the sentences that are almost right. She shows what a comma or a tense changes for the reader, so the fix sticks the next time.
Hear Luana
BOOKS, C1 GRAMMAR
Our CEO who joined in March will present the results.
Is this right for an all-hands email?
WHAT THE COMMAS CHANGE
Without commas, the sentence suggests you have more than one CEO and you mean the one who joined in March.
Our CEO, who joined in March, will present the results.
One CEO. The March detail is extra information.
Two commas. One CEO.
EXPRESSIONS
Bia
“That's how people really say it.”
Bia explains the expressions people hear in meetings and Slack, with the closest version in their own language and the situations where each one fits.
Hear Bia
EXPRESSIONS
English to Italian
English to Portuguese
touch base
IN ITALIAN
Closest to fare il punto or sentirsi un attimo.
Let's touch base tomorrow.
Very common at work. Fine with your manager and your team.
Could we have a quick call tomorrow?
Safer with a new client.
Same idea, a different room.
PRONUNCIATION AND LISTENING
Murillo
“Stress the word that matters.”
Murillo gives your people a sentence from real work, listens to them say it and shows exactly where the stress fell. Then they try again.
Hear Murillo
BOOKS, CALIBRATED SPEECH
Say it out loud
I'd like to
present
the results.
Recorded. 4 seconds.
WHAT MURILLO HEARD
You said PRES-ent, the noun. As a verb it is pre-SENT.
The gift is a PRES-ent.
You pre-SENT the results.
Once more, stress on SENT.
WORD ORIGINS
Marcelo
“Every word has a story.”
Marcelo is the intern who digs up where words come from. A word with a story is a word people remember and use with confidence.
Hear Marcelo
WORD ORIGINS
budget
WHERE IT CAME FROM
From the Old French bougette, a small leather bag.
In Britain, the finance minister opened the budget, the bag that held the year's accounts. The word moved from the bag to the plan inside it.
Now you won't forget it.
HOW IT WORKS FOR YOUR COMPANY
Practice in private.
Improve
in public.
What stays with the learner
Conversations with the coaches stay between the learner and the coach. The company never sees an individual's answers or level. People practice the sentence they would never risk in a meeting.
How it fits the lessons
The app picks up what came up in class, so the practice starts where the lesson stopped. Every coach follows the same method as the teacher in the room.
Five situations from real work. No sign-up.
Victor Hugo
REGISTER
QUESTION 1 OF 5
A client's invoice is three weeks late. Which message do you send?
You want the payment and you want to keep the client.
Just a friendly reminder that invoice 214 is now overdue.
Polite on the surface. Many clients read “friendly reminder” as a warning, and it asks for nothing specific.
As per my last email, invoice 214 is overdue.
Tells the client they ignored you. It gets read as irritation, and it puts the relationship on the table.
Could you let me know when we can expect payment on invoice 214?
Asks for a date instead of an apology. It keeps the door open and gets you a commitment.
That one lands.
That one slips.
Next question
Luana
GRAMMAR AND PUNCTUATION
QUESTION 2 OF 5
This sentence opens your report to the board. Which version would a careful editor leave alone?
The board reads every word. You want them reading the numbers.
Fewer clients renewed this quarter than last.
Clean. “Fewer” goes with things you can count, like clients.
Less clients renewed this quarter than last.
Common in speech, so it sounds fine. In writing to a board, some readers will stop on it.
Less clients have renewed this quarter compared to last.
Same slip, plus a longer comparison that weakens the number.
That one lands.
That one slips.
Next question
Bia
EXPRESSIONS
QUESTION 3 OF 5
A client says your proposal is “not quite there yet.” What is the client telling you?
You want to know whether to edit or rethink.
It's almost ready. A few small edits will do.
The literal reading. In business English this phrase is usually softer than what it means.
It needs real changes before the client will say yes.
The polite way of saying no to this version. The client is still open, but small edits will not get you there.
The client is rejecting the proposal.
Too far. A client who was done would not say “yet.”
That one lands.
That one slips.
Next question
Murillo
PRONUNCIATION AND LISTENING
QUESTION 4 OF 5
You are correcting a date on a call. Which word carries the stress?
You want the correction to be the first thing they hear.
The MEETING is on Thursday, not Tuesday.
Stresses the wrong idea. Nobody doubted it was a meeting.
The meeting is on THURSDAY, not Tuesday.
The new day is the news, so it carries the stress.
The meeting IS on Thursday, not Tuesday.
Sounds like an argument about whether the meeting exists.
That one lands.
That one slips.
Next question
Marcelo
WORD ORIGINS
QUESTION 5 OF 5
The word “deadline” first meant...
Every word has a story. This one starts in the 1860s.
A line in a prison camp that prisoners were not allowed to cross.
First recorded in the United States in the 1860s. Printers later used it for the edge of the printable area, and newsrooms turned it into a time.
The last train of the day.
A good guess, but the railways had nothing to do with it.
The date a contract expires.
That came much later, once “deadline” already meant a time limit.
That one lands.
That one slips.
See your result

## https://theconceptmethod.com/method.html

Try the Method: Six Short Demonstrations | The Concept Method
THE METHOD, LIVE
Don't read the method.
Run it
on yourself.
This page is not a description of how I teach. It is a compressed version of an actual lesson, with you as the student. Six short demonstrations. Nothing to install, nothing to submit, no data leaves your browser.
About 6 minutes
Works on your phone
Your answers stay local
WHERE EVERYONE ELSE STARTS
The Communicative Approach is
table stakes
, not a differentiator.
i.
What every school sells you
Language is learned by using it, not by studying it. Lessons run in English, students speak from minute one, grammar serves the task instead of the other way round. This has been the industry standard since the 1980s, and it works. I use it too. Any provider who does not is simply behind.
ii.
Where it stops being enough
The Communicative Approach optimises for one thing: getting the message across. In a negotiation, getting the message across is the floor, not the ceiling. Your client understood the sentence perfectly. They just trusted you slightly less afterwards, and neither of you can say exactly why. That gap is what the next three sections are about.
Every school teaches your team to be understood. I train them to be believed.
THE TRIPLE A CYCLE
One real message,
three
beats.
Every lesson I teach runs the same cycle: Access, Analysis, Activation. Below it runs on one authentic email, the kind your sales team gets on a Tuesday. Do it in order.
A1
Access
Access means meeting the language where it actually lives: a message that was really sent, not one written for a coursebook. Nothing here is simplified. This is the raw material.
CLICK THE THREE UNDERLINED PHRASES
From: Elena Rossi · Procurement · Subject: Revised quote
Hi Marco,
Thanks for the revised quote.
To be honest
, we were expecting something closer to the figure we discussed in June.
I'd hate for this to stall over 8%
.
Could you have another look?
Best,
Elena
A2
Analysis
Now the reply. Your position is fixed: the price does not move. Same message, five registers, from frozen to intimate. Only one of them holds the price and keeps the client.
MOVE ACROSS THE FIVE REGISTERS
Warmth
0
Authority
0
WHAT IT COSTS YOU
This is the step every other method skips. Meaning is where they stop. I do not stop until the register is right, because your client is not grading the meaning.
A3
Activation
Language you have understood is not language you can use. Activation is the moment I put it under pressure, because pressure is the only condition your team will ever actually use it in.
20 SECONDS. PICK YOUR LINE.
MARCO REPLIES
"I understand. Let me be direct: we have another quote 8% below yours. I'd rather work with you. Help me justify that internally."
Start the clock
20
TIME LEFT
You just did all three steps. Access gave you the raw language, Analysis gave you the map, Activation put it under load. Roughly forty five minutes of this, once or twice a week, on your team's actual emails.
THE PART NOBODY ELSE SELLS
Your team's English is not broken.
The retrieval
is.
Psycholinguistics is the study of how language is stored and retrieved in the brain. It is why people who read contracts in English every day go silent the moment the stakes rise. Four demonstrations. Run them on yourself, honestly, and notice how it feels rather than how you score.
01
Storage: you do not store words. You store neighbourhoods.
A native speaker does not build “make a decision” out of a verb and a noun. They pull the whole phrase off the shelf, already assembled. Learners build it every single time, and building costs milliseconds.
SIX PAIRS. PICK THE NATURAL ONE, FAST.
Start
0
Your average, in milliseconds
0
Correct out of 6
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR TEAM
02
Interference: your first language is still in the room.
When two words compete, the faster one wins, and the faster one is usually the one that sounds like your mother tongue. This is not carelessness. It is a race, and the wrong runner is closer to the finish line.
PICK A LANGUAGE. TAP EACH TRAP.
Italian speakers
Portuguese speakers
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR TEAM
None of these people lack vocabulary. They know the correct word. It simply loses the race, every time, under pressure. A word list will not fix that, because the list is not what is failing. What changes it is repeated retrieval under load, which is precisely what the Activation step is for.
03
Load: this is why the room goes quiet.
Working memory holds about four things at once. In a negotiation your team is already holding the numbers, the client's last objection, and their boss's red line. Then they need a conditional.
HOLD FIVE DIGITS. ANSWER ONE QUESTION. GIVE THE DIGITS BACK.
Start
MEMORIZE THESE. FOUR SECONDS.
NOW TYPE THE FIVE DIGITS
Check
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR TEAM
Something always drops, and it is never the numbers. It is the language, because the language is the only part still charging you rent. This is why I train to automaticity and not to correctness. Correct English that costs attention is English that vanishes at the exact moment the stakes arrive.
04
Emotion: the tone lands before the sentence ends.
Listeners register the emotional charge of a message before they have finished processing its content. Your client felt something about the sentence before they reached the verb. Three messages, identical information.
TAP EACH ONE
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOUR TEAM
This is the emotional layer, and it decides whether your client leans in or leans back. It is measurable, it is teachable, and it has never once appeared on any exam your team has passed.
THE LABELS, TRANSLATED
What I would call this in a lecture. What it means to you.
The first three are craft. The fourth is the reason a fluent team still loses the room, and the reason you are on this page.
NEXT STEP
Now run it on
your team
.
Everything you just did, I do live, with your people, on their actual emails and their actual calls. Forty five minutes, no charge, no obligation. I tell you exactly where they break down under pressure, and whether training is even worth your budget.
Pedro Gigollotti · Teacher and Academic Director · São Paulo · Rome · Milano

Business English Books and Manuals | The Concept Method
The Concept Method
One collection.
One Method.
Professional English Practice takes you from your first words to full command of the language, book by book. Calibrated Speech does the same for how you sound while you say it.
Professional English Practice
Four books, one continuous system, from your first sentence in English to full C2 command, plus a dedicated book on the phrasal verbs that trip up even fluent professionals.
Professional English Practice · Book 1 · CEFR A1-A2
It's Not Only a Grammar Book
English Communication for Professionals
Forty-four units repair the grammar you already half know: the verb to be, the present, the past, the three futures, the modals, and the relative clause that lets you stop speaking in short separate sentences. Each unit prints the wrong sentence beside the right one, because you cannot stop making a mistake you have never seen written down.
For the professional who is told he is a beginner and knows he is not. You read the email, you follow the meeting, and then somebody turns and asks you something and the words are gone. They were there yesterday. Nothing you say is broken enough for anyone to correct, so nobody ever has.
Introduce yourself and your work with confidence
Handle greetings, requests, and everyday small talk
Turn memorized phrases into words you actually mean
Speak your first real conversations without freezing
Online now
Students: access the interactive units →
Professional English Practice · Book 2 · CEFR B1-B2
It's Not Only a Grammar Book
English Communication for Professionals
Forty units carry you through the machinery of real fluency: the full past and future systems, the unreal and the hypothetical, modality and deduction, the advanced passive and reported speech, and the structures that let you emphasize, concede, and read the room.
For professionals who can already get by, but want to stop simplifying to stay safe and start steering the conversation instead.
From getting by to saying what you actually mean
Explaining and justifying your reasoning, not just stating it
Holding your own when the meeting speeds up
Online now

Professional English Practice · Book 3 · CEFR C1
It's Not Only a Grammar Book
English Communication for Professionals
Thirty-six units move through the verb system, modality, emphasis, cohesion, reporting, and register, ending in the reformulation and lexical control that mark real fluency, built for the whole professional world, not only executives.
At C1 the grammar is mostly there; what's missing is control. This book is about the choices that carry weight: who a sentence blames, how certain you sound, what lands first and last. Accuracy becomes strategy.
Control tone, stance, and emphasis on purpose
Concede ground without losing your position
Foreground the one thing that matters
Report and attribute with precision

Professional English Practice · Book 4 · CEFR C2
It's Not Only a Grammar Book
English Communication for Professionals
Twenty-two units move from aspect and formal conditionals through modality, marked word order, cohesion, and reporting, ending in the competence that defines the level: saying the same thing three different ways, on purpose, for three different audiences.
C2 is the C1 canon revisited for nuance: reformulation, marked structure, irony and understatement, the exact shade of a near-synonym. This book is about saying the same thing three ways and choosing the one the moment needs.
Reformulate the same idea three ways
Use inversion and clefts for rhetorical effect
Say less to mean more: irony, litotes, understatement
Choose the word with the exact weight
Online now
Students: access the interactive units →
Professional English Practice · Book 5 · CEFR B1-C2
It's Not Only a Phrasal Verb List
English Communication for Professionals
Organized by particle rather than topic: the same handful of particles, like up, out, and off, recur across dozens of verbs with a traceable core meaning, so recognition transfers instead of resetting with every new verb.
Every other phrasal verb book hands you an endless list and asks you to memorize it. The list never ends, so learners give up and reach for the stiff Latinate word instead. This book does the opposite: you learn twenty particles, not two thousand verbs, and the meaning falls out of the particle. You stop recalling. You start predicting.
Read the particle and predict a verb you've never seen
Choose the phrasal verb a native would use, not the Latinate one
Catch phrasal verbs in fast speech instead of missing them
Turn twenty particles into hundreds of verbs you can deploy
Online now
Students: access the interactive units →
Calibrated Speech
A pronunciation manual sequenced A1 to C2, built on two yardsticks: being understood, and being taken seriously.
Calibrated Speech · CEFR A1-C2
Calibrated Speech
American English for Brazilian Speakers
A level-by-level pronunciation manual sequenced A1 to C2, built on two yardsticks, intelligibility and credibility. Moves from the sounds that break meaning, th, clean final consonants, ship versus sheep, through rhythm and the American R, to the melody and register control that read as credible to American listeners.
For Brazilian Portuguese speakers whose message lands, but whose accent still shapes how seriously they're taken in the room.
Sound-by-sound sequencing, A1 to C2
Diagnostic passage and a fastest-fixes cheat sheet
Full practice sets with a complete answer key

## https://theconceptmethod.com/library/professional-english-practice-a1-a2/

It's Not Only a Grammar Book, A1-A2 | The Concept Method
Professional English Practice · Book 1
It's Not Only a Grammar Book
A1-A2
English Communication for Professionals
Professional English Practice · Book 1 · CEFR A1-A2
English Communication for Professionals
Forty-four units repair the grammar you already half know: the verb to be, the present, the past, the three futures, the modals, and the relative clause that lets you stop speaking in short separate sentences. Each unit prints the wrong sentence beside the right one, because you cannot stop making a mistake you have never seen written down.
For the professional who is told he is a beginner and knows he is not. You read the email, you follow the meeting, and then somebody turns and asks you something and the words are gone. They were there yesterday. Nothing you say is broken enough for anyone to correct, so nobody ever has.
Introduce yourself and your work with confidence
Handle greetings, requests, and everyday small talk
Turn memorized phrases into words you actually mean
Speak your first real conversations without freezing

It's Not Only a Grammar Book
B1-B2

Professional English Practice · Book 2 · CEFR B1-B2
English Communication for Professionals
Forty units carry you through the machinery of real fluency: the full past and future systems, the unreal and the hypothetical, modality and deduction, the advanced passive and reported speech, and the structures that let you emphasize, concede, and read the room.
For professionals who can already get by, but want to stop simplifying to stay safe and start steering the conversation instead.
From getting by to saying what you actually mean
Explaining and justifying your reasoning, not just stating it
Holding your own when the meeting speeds up
